paper_title: TauIndianBankBench: Procedure-Aware, Action-Oriented Evaluation of Tool-Using Conversational Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots. Assistants based on language models could respond faster and carry out requests such as blocking a card, but only if they give correct information and follow the bank's rules. These rules prescribe a procedure, a set of required steps, such as obtaining a closure quote before closing a deposit. Adapting models to this domain requires measuring how well they follow the procedure, before and after training. Benchmarks usually judge only the records left at the end of a conversation. Many required steps, however, leave the records unchanged, so an assistant that skips them can still be judged successful. We present TauIndianBankBench, an action-oriented benchmark of 1,000 Indian retail-banking tasks where an assistant helps a simulated customer. Besides the final records, it checks that the assistant took every required step and made no unrequested change. For every model, 6.5-12.0% of sessions are judged successful when only the final records are checked, although the assistant skipped a required step or made an unrequested change. Scoring both procedure and outcome shows more accurately how well language models perform in Indian retail banking.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Many Indian banks serve customers through FAQ pages and scripted chatbots that return fixed answers. Assistants based on language models could respond faster, answer questions that no FAQ anticipates, and carry out requests such as blocking card or booking deposit. bank can rely on such an assistant only if it gives correct information and follows the banks rules, because an error affects the customer directly. Adapting model to this domain, for example by training it, therefore requires benchmark that measures how well the model serves customers, both before and after training. 1 Several benchmarks evaluate language models as customer-service agents that use tools to retrieve records, apply written policy, and make changes (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025a). These benchmarks usually check the resulting records rather than the transcript, because an assistant may describe blocking compromised card in fluent prose without calling the tool that blocks it, and metric that can be satisfied without doing the work can be gamed (Skalse et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2025). Checking the final records has its own limitation, however: written policy prescribes procedure of required steps, and many of these steps leave the records unchanged. Before closing deposit, the assistant must obtain closure quote so that the customer knows the penalty (Figure 1). Before booking deposit that the balance may not support, it must look up the banks minimum-balance rule. Before blocking card, it must check the cards status. An assistant that skips these steps still produces the correct records and passes final-state check, but the customer does not receive the information that these steps are meant to provide. In Indian retail banking, regulation states many required steps explicitly: know-your-customer (KYC) verification must be renewed periodically (Reserve Bank of India, 2016), deposit interest is subject to tax deducted at source (TDS) with prescribed exemption forms, and government savings schemes have statutory eligibility rules. Our tasks turn the banks written policy for servicing requests, such as closing deposit or applying seniorcitizen rate, into required steps, most of which are reads. In our corpus, 962 of the 1,000 released tasks require at least one read-only call, and 114 require no write call. Existing Indian and financial evaluation suites assess language coverage, domain knowledge, numerical reasoning, or financial tool use, but not customer servicing under Indian banking rules (2). We therefore introduce TauIndianBankBench,1 an action-oriented benchmark of Indian retailbanking servicing (3.1). It comprises synthetic bank, catalogue of servicing tools, written policy, knowledge base that covers these regulations, and 1,000 tasks, from which smaller train and test splits are drawn for adapting model to the domain. It runs in the 𝜏2-bench harness (Barres et al., 2026), an extension of 𝜏-bench (Yao et al., 2025). In this harness, the assistant under evaluation talks with simulated customer, itself language model, and acts on shared database. Tasks fall into four categories. Sequencing tasks require several dependent calls (up to six). Edge-case tasks contain condition that the assistant must recognise before acting, such as an ineligible or ambiguous request. Rare-tool tasks use infrequently needed operations. Control tasks are straightforward requests and serve as an internal baseline. Each session receives two pass/fail verdicts (3.2). The final-state check, inherited from 𝜏bench and 𝜏2-bench, compares the final records with those produced by replaying the tasks gold chain, its reference sequence of tool calls. The action check extends the action matching of 𝜏2-bench. It requires every call in the gold chain, including reads, to appear in the session. Its write purity condition fails the session if the assistant makes any change that the task did not request. Our headline measure is the pass rate, the share of sessions judged successful; session passes only if both checks pass. We evaluate six open-weight models, five from the Gemma 4 family (Gemma Team, 2026) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), with the same simulated customer, and report two findings (5). First, the final-state check accepts procedural violations for every model: it passes sessions in which the assistant omitted required call or made an unrequested change (5.2). Second, each check fails sessions that the other passes. For the three strongest models, most sessions that fail exactly one check are procedural violations, which only the action check detects. For the weakest model, most such sessions include every gold-chain call yet end with incorrect records, which only the final-state check detects (5.3). Two further results support the validity of this pass criterion. Trivial scripted agents pass no task (5.7), and control-task pass 1Code: github.com/npci/TauIndianBankBench; dataset: huggingface.co/datasets/NPCI/tau-indian-banking. rates show no trend with model size, whereas the three graded categories separate the models (5.6). Our contributions are as follows: (1) an Indian retail-banking environment with synthetic bank, servicing tools, and tasks derived from written policy (3.1); (2) an action check that complements the final-state check by scoring required reads and penalising unrequested changes (3.2); and (3) an evaluation of six models under both checks, showing that the final-state check alone gives an incomplete measure of how well models follow the procedure (5). We release the code, data, and reference results.

sections.content: Conversational and enterprise tool-use benchmarks. Function-calling benchmarks evaluate API selection and arguments, from ToolLLMs more than 16,000 real APIs (Qin et al., 2024) to the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (Patil et al., 2025) and ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025). AgentBench evaluates models as agents across eight environments (Liu et al., 2024), API-Bank evaluates API planning and calling in annotated dialogues (Li et al., 2023), and ToolTalk specifies multi-step intents through dialogue (Farn and Interactive and enterprise benchShin, 2023). marks execute the agent and assess the outcome: WebArena and Mind2Web on web tasks (Zhou et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2023), WorkArena on 2 ServiceNow knowledge work (Drouin et al., 2024), and CRMArena and CRMArena-Pro on customerrelationship tasks, the latter with persona-driven users (Huang et al., 2025a,b). AppWorld additionally checks for collateral damage, that is, unrequested changes (Trivedi et al., 2024), and Thinkingbox rejects wrong, missing, or extra effects in the terminal state of business workflows (Li et al., 2026). These interactive benchmarks assess what the agent changed; they cannot detect required step that modifies no records. Process and policy-compliance scoring. Other work scores the individual steps of an agent. TRAJECT-Bench checks tool choice, arguments, and dependency order against reference trajectories (He et al., 2025), TRACE scores reasoning steps without reference (Kim et al., 2026), and EgoBench validates both process and result (Liu et al., 2026). For mathematical reasoning, reward models trained with step-level supervision outperform those trained only on final answers (Lightman et al., 2024). ST-WebAgentBench credits only policycompliant completions (Levy et al., 2026), SOPBench builds tasks from expert-written standard operating procedures (Nandi et al., 2025), and IntellAgent generates test conversations from policy graph (Levi and Kadar, 2025). ToolSandbox is the closest design (Lu et al., 2025). It checks required milestones, including specific tool calls, and forbidden minefields. Its milestone score, however, gives partial credit for similarity to the expected session, including message text, and minefields must be written for each task. JourneyBench (Balaji et al., 2026) scores conversation zero if any tool call is missing, extra, or out of order, but its tools return pre-generated responses, so it cannot check whether the calls produced the correct records. Our benchmark combines shared database and final-state check with an action check that requires policy-mandated reads and enforces write purity (3.2). We apply both checks to every session and measure the gap between them (5). Table 3 (Appendix A) summarises these designs. Financial and Indian-language benchmarks. Most financial LLM benchmarks test knowledge and numerical reasoning: broad suites such as FinBen, PIXIU, and FinEval (Xie et al., 2024, 2023; Guo et al., 2025), numerical and table reasoning (Chen et al., 2021, 2022; Zhu et al., 2021; Krumdick et al., 2024), and deposit and loan arithmetic (Lee et al., 2026). The Finance Agent Benchmark, FinToolBench, and FinMCP-Bench let the model call tools (Bigeard et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026). Evaluation in the Indian context has focused on Indian languages (Kakwani et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2022; Doddapaneni et al., 2023) and India-specific knowledge (Verma et al., 2025), with bilingual finance subset in BhashaBench (Devane et al., 2025). Validity of agent evaluation. The agentic benchmark checklist of Zhu et al. (2025) recommends trivial-agent baselines to expose scores that can be obtained without performing the task. An audit of tool-calling benchmarks identifies brittle state matching and trajectory lock-in (Bhat et al., 2026). LLM-simulated users can misestimate agent success (Seshadri et al., 2026), and agents degrade when users do not cooperate (Shim et al., 2026). Judge models exhibit position, verbosity, and selfpreference biases (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023), which motivates deterministic scoring.

sections.title: 3.1 Environment and tasks
sections.content: Simulated bank. session is one conversation on one task between the assistant (the agent under evaluation) and the simulated customer. Each session runs on fresh copy of synthetic bank of 944 customers, each with accounts, cards, deposits, loans, standing instructions, KYC status, and transaction history. The clock is fixed and generated identifiers are seeded, so the replay of the gold chain used for scoring (3.2) starts from the same bank state as the session. The assistant receives the banks written policy and can search, by keyword, 24 knowledge-base documents on payment limits, KYC renewal, deposit insurance, tax on interest, chargeback timelines, and government schemes. It has access to 34 tools: 33 servicing tools for accounts, deposits, loans, cards, mandates (standing payment authorisations), cheques, and service requests, and one that transfers the customer to human staff member. Thirteen servicing tools are writes. Eleven of them change records; the other two request cheque book or duplicate statement without changing any record, and the scorer treats them as writes like the rest. The remaining twenty servicing tools only retrieve data (reads; Table 4, Appendix B). Task specification. Each task fixes the session date and names the logged-in customer but with3 holds the customers profile, so the assistant must retrieve accounts, cards, and products through the tools. Each task also specifies the simulated customers persona and scenario. Finally, each task specifies its gold chain: the reference sequence of tool calls that resolves the request, together with the arguments each call must match. Gold chains contain 3.54 calls on average and range from one to six (per-length counts in Table 11, Appendix G.2). Appendix reproduces one released task. Task categories and service areas. The tasks are drawn from 50 task families, groups of tasks that share request type (listed in Table 7). The families fall into four categories (Table 5, Appendix D): three graded categories designed to be difficult, and control category of simple requests that serves as baseline. By subject, the tasks fall into four service areas: everyday banking (balances, mandates, cheques, service requests), deposits, loans (instalments, foreclosure quotes, gold loans), and cards (controls, blocking, disputes). Data splits. The release defines four splits: base (1,000 tasks), on which all reference results are computed; lite, subset of 200 tasks, four from each family, for faster evaluation; and train (150) and test (50), which partition lite. Scores from different splits are not comparable, and method tuned on the train split should report its results on the test split. Task construction and validation. language model drafted the tasks against the live environment, and task was admitted only if it passed four filters. The first filter enforces varied first messages. Within family, no first message may occur in more than 40% of the tasks, and at least eight distinct ones are required. This prevents model from identifying the family instead of interpreting the request. The second requires gold chain of at least three calls for graded tasks. The third ensures that no task appears in both the train and test splits. The fourth admits task only if its replayed gold chain passes both checks (3.2).

sections.title: 3.2 Scoring
sections.content: A session is scored deterministically by two pass/fail checks. The action check examines the trajectory, the record of every message and tool call; the final-state check examines the final database. The final-state check is inherited from 𝜏-bench and 𝜏2-bench (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026), and the requirement that each gold-chain call appear in the session comes from the action matching of 𝜏2-bench. We add two components (2): the gold chain includes the reads that the policy requires, and write purity requires every write to match gold-chain write. Pass criterion. session scores 1 if both checks pass and 0 otherwise, and session that scores 1 passes. The pass rate is the headline score of the release (column All of Table 1); unless stated otherwise, every score in 5 is pass rate. session thus passes exactly when it ends normally (4), the assistant makes every gold-chain call and no unrequested change, and the final records match the expected ones. No partial credit is given: session that makes three of four required calls scores 0, the same as one that does nothing. Appendix gives the pseudocode. Final-state check. Oracle replay runs the tasks gold chain on the same seeded starting records to produce the expected final records, and the finalstate check compares the sessions final records with them. Before the comparison, the scorer normalises both: it removes fields that change from run to run (generated references, download links, free-text notes) and ignores the position of entries in collections keyed by generated identifiers. On service requests, it also ignores the optional account and treats the two general request categories as one. Timestamps need no removal, because the environment runs on fixed clock. The scorer then compares hashes of the normalised records, so records match when their content is identical, regardless of their byte-level representation. The check therefore observes only the outcome: because reads modify no records, it cannot detect an omitted read, and on task that requires no change, any session that makes no change passes it. The action check addresses this limitation. Action check. The action check searches the session for each gold-chain call, regardless of the order in which the calls were made. Each gold-chain call specifies which of its arguments must match. If it lists some arguments, only those are compared. If its argument list is empty, only the tool name is compared. If it has no argument list, every argument given in the gold-chain call is compared, except run-dependent identifiers and free-text fields, which carry no information about correctness. An optional account identifier is compared only when check verifies the result. Scorer audit. We compared the released scorer with an independent re-implementation of the scorer on 600 recorded sessions; the two implementations gave the same verdicts on every session and on all 705 paired tool calls. Before release, the packaged scorer also re-scored 5,000 recorded sessions and reproduced every score exactly. The model ranking (5) was also reproduced on second model-serving setup, with score differences no larger than those between repeated runs. The harnesss judge model, which grades the conversation text and does not affect the released score, gives the same verdict as the re-implementation on 87.5% of sessions and gives less credit in every disagreement (Table 8, Appendix F).

sections.title: 4 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Conversation protocol. session alternates between the assistant and the customer. On each turn, the assistant either sends one message to the customer or makes one or more tool calls, but not both. The session ends when the customer states that the request is resolved, or when the assistant ends the session or transfers the customer to human staff member. session that reaches the limit of 200 steps or 10 failed tool calls, or stops because of an error, scores 0. language model plays the customer. It is prompted with the tasks persona and scenario and fixed set of instructions. It reveals information step by step and does not name tools or say which call to make. In graded tasks, it asks for the steps in the listed order and asks the assistant to return to step it skipped. Reporting. Because the customer simulator shapes every conversation, we report the assistant model, the customer-simulator model, and the split together, and compare only runs that share all three. Throughout this paper, MiniMax-M2.7 (MiniMax, 2026) plays the customer at temperature zero, so that the customers side of every conversation can be reproduced. run may attempt each task 𝑘 times to estimate pass𝑘, the probability that all 𝑘 attempts at task pass. The reference results use one attempt per task on the full base split, and Appendix G.4 analyses second attempt.

Because the gold chain includes the required reads, session that omits one fails the action check even when its final records are correct (Figure 1). If the assistant closes the wrong Write purity. deposit or freezes card the customer did not mention, write purity fails the session even if every gold-chain call was also made. This prevents an assistant from passing by issuing every available call. The rule also applies when the change is later undone: the final-state check then passes, but write purity fails the session, because the customer was affected while the change was in place. Call order. The task design fixes the order of the required steps in two ways (column Order of Table 3). First, some calls need values that only an earlier call returns: in the task of Appendix C, the maturity projection needs the rate that the rate-card call returns, so it can match the gold chain only after that call. Second, in every task outside the control category, the simulated customers instructions list the requests as numbered steps, which the customer raises one at time and in order. In the same task, for instance, the customer agrees to book the deposit only after seeing the projected maturity value. sections.title: 5.1 Reference results
sections.content: Table 1 reports the reference results. Among the four dense Gemma models, each larger model passes more tasks than the next smaller one (𝑝 < 0.005 for each pair, paired sign test). This ranking also holds within each of the three graded categories (Figure 3, Appendix G).

sections.title: 5.2 Violations missed by the final-state check
sections.content: We score every session twice: with the final-state check alone, as in 𝜏-bench, and with both checks, as in the headline score. session that passes the former but fails the latter ended with the correct records but either omitted required call or made an unrequested change; we refer to such session as procedural violation (Table 2; Figure 4, Appendix G). Scoring only the final records raises each models pass rate by 6.512.0 points, the share of its sessions that are procedural violations. sections.title: 5.4 Performance by task category
sections.content: The categories differ in what they require and in how widely they separate the models; Table 6 (Appendix D) summarises their composition. Sequencing. Sequencing tasks (470 tasks in 20 families; Table 7) require several dependent calls. Although their gold chains are the shortest among the graded categories (3.64 calls on average; 279 tasks require three calls), this category separates the models most widely, from 0.455 for E2B to 0.921 for Qwen3.8-27B. Edge cases. Edge-case tasks (266 tasks in 14 families; Table 7) each contain condition that the assistant must recognise before acting (Appendix groups these families). Every edge-case gold chain contains at least one write, so the assistant must both handle the exception and complete the legitimate part of the request. Every model scores lower on edge cases than on sequencing, with pass rates from 0.426 (E2B) to 0.774 (Qwen3.8-27B). Rare tools. Rare-tool tasks (152 tasks in 8 families; Table 7) are each built around an infrequently required operation, such as deposit maturity projection, the status of an earlier service request, or the details of an insurance policy. None of these eight tools appears in more than 56 of the 1,000 gold chains. This is the lowest-scoring category for every model. The Gemma models fall within narrow range (0.3880.559), whereas Qwen3.8-27B exceeds the 31B by 0.198, its largest margin over that model in any category.

sections.title: 5.7 Trivial-agent baselines
sections.content: We evaluated four scripted agents, none of which passes any task. The first only replies to the customer, the second looks up records but makes no required call, and the third claims in persuasive message that the work is complete; all three fail the action check. The fourth makes every available change and fails write purity.

sections.title: 5.8 Further analyses
sections.content: Appendix G.3 classifies failed sessions by type. Stopping short of the full procedure is the most frequent type for every model. Unrequested writes make up larger share of failures for the strongest models, and sessions that finish with errors make up larger share for the weakest. second run of the five Gemma models changes each pass rate by at most 2.7 points, although 1426% of tasks change outcome between the two runs (Appendix G.4).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Tasks that require more calls are not uniformly harder: four-call tasks are the hardest for every model except E2B. The gap between the strongest and the weakest model is widest on five-call tasks (0.614, against 0.024 on one-call tasks). Within the sequencing and edge-case categories, long tasks affect the weakest models most. For example, E4B falls from 0.810 on short sequencing tasks to 0.445 on long ones, whereas none of the three strongest models changes by more than 0.086 on sequencing or edge-case tasks. On rare-tool tasks, by contrast, Qwen3.8-27B declines most, from 0.923 to 0.699 (Appendix G.2).

sections.title: 5.6 Control category
sections.content: The control category (112 tasks, 1.38 calls on average, 93 with no write) allows us to exclude an alternative explanation, namely that the graded categories reward general capability rather than competence in banking procedure. Under that explanation, pass rates on the simple control requests would also increase with model size. Across the four dense Gemma models, however, they remain between 0.804 and 0.929 without trend in size, and the highest rate belongs to the 12B, whereas sequencing pass rates increase with size (5.1; Figure 3). The categories that require multi-step procedures thus rank the models by size, whereas the control category does not. Assistants based on language models could serve the customers of Indian banks, but only if they follow the banks procedure as well as reach the correct result. Scoring only the final records gives an incomplete measure of this, because many required steps do not change the records. TauIndianBankBench adds an action check that scores these steps. The final-state check alone accepts procedural violations for every model, and each check fails sessions that the other passes. We therefore recommend that benchmarks for service assistants in regulated domains report an action check alongside the final-state check, and that model adapted to Indian retail banking be measured with both checks before and after training, for which the release provides separate train and test splits. The benchmark is distributed as standard domain of the 𝜏2-bench harness (Barres et al., 2026) and runs against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: First, score depends on both the assistant and the simulated customer (4); the reported numbers therefore hold only for the simulator we used, whose own error rate we did not measure. Second, all customer data are synthetic, so the frequency of each type of edge case reflects our generated records rather than actual bank traffic. Third, version 1.0.0 covers Indian retail banking in English only; other languages and domains are left to future 7 versions. Finally, evaluation is computationally costly. Every session is live multi-turn conversation in which both the assistant and the simulated customer are language models. single run on the base split therefore requires 1,000 such conversations of up to 200 steps each, and estimating pass𝑘 multiplies this cost by 𝑘. When either model is served through commercial API, full evaluation incurs substantial inference cost. The 200-task lite split is provided for development and ablations, and the base split for final reporting of untuned models.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: All customer data in the benchmark are synthetic, and the records contain no field for national identification number. Email addresses and phone numbers are generated placeholders; all organisation and place names are invented, and we verified that none matches real one. The benchmark is intended for research on and evaluation of tool-using agents and does not constitute financial advice. pass indicates only that, with our simulated customer, the assistant made the required calls, made no unrequested change, and left the records correct. It does not establish that the assistant is suitable for deployment in bank, which would require further safety, privacy, and regulatory review.

sections.title: C Example Task
sections.content: Figure 2 reproduces task rl_tlfdmat_0197 as released in tasks.json. The simulated customer is senior citizen who prefers explanations without jargon. The customer requests fixed deposit (FD) of Rs. 2,00,000 for 12 months, but only after reviewing the maturity value projected from the current rate card, and then asks to see the savings balance after the debit. The customers instructions are written for the simulator and are never shown to the assistant, which must obtain each detail through the conversation and the tools. The gold chain lists five calls; for two of them, compare_args restricts argument matching to the named fields. Three of the four distinct calls are reads: the account balance, the FD rate card, and the maturity projection at the quoted 7.3% rate. The final balance read repeats the first, so single balance read satisfies both (3.2). Since create_fd is the only write, the final-state check observes only its effects: the new deposit and the debit from the savings account. Only the action check can therefore determine whether the assistant consulted the rate card and projected the maturity value. 11 { } "id": "rl_tlfdmat_0197", "description": { "purpose": "Balance -> rate -> maturity calc -> create FD -> balance ...", ... }, "user_scenario": { "persona": "You are senior citizen who prefers clear, patient explanations ...", "instructions": { "domain": "banking", "reason_for_call": "You want new FD of Rs.200000 for 12 months, but only after seeing the projected maturity value ...", "known_info": "... Fam.: task families  (Table 7)  . Mean: mean number of calls in the gold chain (graded categories 36 calls, control 13). Short / long: tasks with at most three and with four or more gold-chain calls. Reads: share of gold-chain calls that are reads. Write: tasks whose gold chain contains at least one write. Table 7 lists all 50 families. The 14 edge-case families fall into four groups, according to the condition that the assistant must handle. The first group (4 families, 76 tasks) requires declining an invalid or unsafe request, such as repeating an irreversible card block, applying benefit for which the customer is ineligible, skipping confirmation under pressure, or disclosing internal codes. The second (5 families, 93 tasks) requires correcting or clarifying information supplied by the customer, such as misremembered mandate number, an account that is not on record, an unspecified card, statement period that precedes the accounts opening, or changed tenure. The third (2 families, 40 tasks) requires applying the correct action to each of several similar cards or mandates. The fourth (3 families, 57 tasks) requires limiting commitment to what the account supports. No gold chain includes transfer to human staff member. Each rare-tool family centres on one of eight tools (get_account_details, calculate_fd_maturity, calculate_rd_maturity, calculate_gold_loan_ltv, get_insurance_details, get_products_and_offers, get_rd_details, get_request_status). Each of these tools appears in at least 19 gold chains, and calculate_fd_maturity and get_request_status appear only in rare-tool tasks.

G.3 Failure types We measure the fraction of gold-chain calls that each session made and assign every failed session to one of three types (Table 13 and Figure 6). session that stopped short ended or was handed off before the procedure was complete. session with an unrequested write made change that the task did not request. session that finished with errors called every tool in the gold chain but used incorrect arguments in at least one call, or ended with incorrect records. Stopping short accounts for 49.664.0% of failed sessions. The other two types vary in opposite directions. Unrequested writes account for 34.4% of failures for Qwen3.8-27B and 29.0% for the 31B, but for only 9.713.5% for the three weakest models. Finishing with errors accounts for 13.815.9% for the three strongest models and 28.236.9% for the three weakest.
